title: Sery Dol
author: Nikolai Pokush
description:
On the border between two mighty empires, far from bustling cities, endless wars, and palace intrigues, lies the Gray Valley—a quiet land of pale mists and ancient forests. Five soldiers’ families have found refuge here. The fathers long ago traded their swords for plows, and their children have grown up knowing nothing of war.

But everything changes in a single night when the daughters of the veteran Sain are attacked by a yellow-eyed monster from ancient folk tales. Young Zana is wounded—the creature’s bite won’t heal. She is tormented by a bestial hunger, and a mysterious call grows louder and louder in her head. To save Zana, her sister must set out to find an old witch living deep in the forest.

Meanwhile, former scout Hanris picks up the beast’s trail but uncovers a far more terrifying threat. Soon it becomes clear to all the valley’s inhabitants: the attack was only the beginning. The ancient beasts have come out to hunt.
Now the veterans must take up arms once more, and their children must grow up far too quickly. 

To protect their homes and families, the heroes will have to face not only the demons of forgotten legends, but also the darkness within themselves.

story.quote: ...The creatures of the night—and tonight, once they catch you, they’ll drag you away. To their lair, in the heart of darkness, and there you’ll vanish forever. I had to tell you this; believe it or not—it’s up to you.

excerpt: Night crept down the mountain slopes. It slid downward in a sluggish wave as the last rays of the dying day vanished behind the western horizon. Enveloping the snow-covered rocky ledges and the peaks of the fluffy fir trees, the night descended into the valley, and with it crept a pale mist—and along with it... something else came into the valley. It lurked in the shadows, gliding as a barely perceptible shadow through the mist, its yellow eyes gleaming—eyes for which the darkness of night posed no barrier—its nostrils flaring and saliva dripping from its mouth. Anticipating the scent of warm blood and desperately longing to sink its teeth into a piece of fresh flesh as soon as possible, it emerged from the darkness of fables and myths, where it had lain hidden for many years, and revealed itself to the slumbering land, whose inhabitants had no idea what awaited them.

It wasn’t people who first sensed it, but the animals living on Saina Gotho’s estate. The sheep began to bleat. The chickens hopped down from their perches and started running in circles around the coop, flapping their wings. The lone cow let out a drawn-out moo. The horses neighed, rearing up and kicking their hooves against the stable walls. Two sheepdogs—old Shaggy and the lively young Fangy, who were locked up for the night in an enclosure next to the barn—began to bark frantically.

Ilya, the eldest of Sain’s daughters, thirteen years old, woke up and immediately sat up in bed, throwing back the down comforter and dangling her feet onto the wooden floor. The room where she slept was filled with thick darkness, but the crackling of the flames could still be heard in the stove standing in the corner, and the room remained warm. That meant the fire hadn’t burned out yet, and therefore, as Ilya quickly realized, the night had only just begun.

Her three sisters, sleeping in the beds next to hers, were also awakened by this incredible noise, which had suddenly burst into the ringing silence of the night. Ilya saw their silhouettes rise one by one from their beds.
“What’s going on?” whimpered four-year-old Riza, who was immediately overcome by the panic she sensed in the animals’ mooing, neighing, barking, and bleating. “Why are they making all that noise?!”

“Hush, hush, sweetheart,” — Ilya rushed over to her little sister, knelt down beside her, and pressed the girl’s head against her chest, feeling her own heart pounding, gripped by a terror whose cause she could not yet understand.
“Where’s Mom?...” Riza’s tantrum was only getting worse. “I want to be with her! I want to be with Mom and Dad!”

“Hush, sweetheart… Shh…” Ilya soothed her sister, clearly sensing how the panic and fear in her mind were growing and spreading. She tried with all her willpower to overcome those feelings, to keep them from taking hold of her, for she was the eldest, and it wasn’t fitting for her to cower in fear in front of her sisters. As she calmed Riza, it was as if she were calming herself as well: “Hush… It’s all right…”

“Something’s going on in the barn,” said Zana, an eleven-year-old girl—the liveliest and bravest of Sain’s daughters—as she pressed her face against the shutters covering the windows. “I think I saw someone on the roof. Maybe a werewolf got in?”
“A werewolf?!” Riza exclaimed in horror, and immediately began crying even harder than before: “Where’s Daddy?! I want to go to Daddy!”
“Have you completely lost your mind, you idiot?!” Ilya snapped at Zana. “What are you talking about?”
Holding Riza closer to her, she whispered in her ear:
— Shh, shh... Zana's talking nonsense. There aren't any werewolves around here.
“Now that’s not nonsense!” Zana retorted, sounding offended. “Remember what Vesna told us about the forests up north and about...”
authorBio: He works as a tester at a manufacturing plant. He’s a big fan of video games and board games, but considers tabletop role-playing games (TRPGs) to be his main hobby. title: In the Dance of Delusions
author: Alexa Dragan
description:
Sasha defies her parents and enrolls in the university of her dreams to become a film director. There, she makes friends, feels like part of the creative world for the first time, and finds a love that feels like destiny to her. 

But love gradually turns into dependence, and creative fulfillment into a painful personal crisis. In search of herself, Sasha flits between lovers, the theater, film shoots, and attempts to prove that she is worthy of the path she has chosen. Every decision brings her closer to her dream, but at the same time distances her from herself.

Years later, the now-adult protagonist returns to this past as if it were an unfinished film. Memories flare up like matches, illuminating what was impossible to understand back then: where love ended and dependence began, where art became salvation, and where it became a way to numb the pain.

A candid psychological novel about first love, creative obsession, coming of age, and the attempt to piece oneself back together after the loss of illusions.

story.quote: Instead of blood, young wine flows through my veins. Don’t be shy—hold out your glasses. I’ll run the blade across my wrists—and fill them to the brim. You’ll be drunk and happy. Just like me.

excerpt:
Where I’m from, people believe in a superstition: don’t look into windows, or you’ll go blind. It’s a silly superstition. My eyesight is still excellent, even though I’ve loved peering into the windows of other people’s homes ever since I was a child. A cat on the windowsill, soup on the stove, awards on the shelf—fragments of another life remain in my memory like a garland of photographs. Who knows when they might come in handy? 
In college, we were taught to record curious observations in a “director’s diary.” We’d read them aloud in class and then try to decipher the psychology behind the behavior of various eccentrics. Once, I myself became the subject of discussion. Sergey looked away sheepishly as he described a stranger at the coffee shop who was scooping the milk foam off her cappuccino with her fingers and immediately licking them. She almost ate the whole coffee. While my classmates argued and came up with hypotheses, I sat huddled in my chair, afraid they’d expose me. At that moment, it felt as if my skin were being scraped with thin blades. 
Today, seventeen years later, it’s as if I’ve found myself back in that same class. 
Vasya managed to gather most of our workshop for the opening of his acting studio. In the years since graduation, we’d scattered across the globe, but by some miracle we all found ourselves in the same city at the same time. Of course, I missed everyone, and congratulating Vasya seemed like a great excuse to catch up with my college friends. Only he hadn’t warned us that we’d be taking part in an impromptu performance.
“Who’s going to start?” Vasya asked, scratching his temple, which was slightly streaked with gray. With age, he’d grown even thinner; even a child’s fingers could have wrapped around his slender wrists. Now he wore glasses.
Time had taken its toll on our lives and faces, though we hadn’t changed all that drastically. If anything, we’d grown a little quieter, faded, worn out. Life had knocked the arrogance out of us, dealt us a few blows, and we’d become much more modest.
Vasya turned off the main light and lit a blood-red lamp shaped like a giant drop. Why make things so complicated? We could have just gotten drunk. 
On the other hand, today is a special date—November 30th. For our ancestors, this was the start of the new year, and in Moldova we honor traditions, so we still celebrate Wolf Day. 
The old fades away, the new takes its place; today, secrets are revealed, prophecies come true, and ghosts come to life. To gain a brave wolf’s soul, one must undergo a rite of passage. It’s a sin to be afraid.
“Since no one else wants to, I’ll go first.”
Red light smeared the walls and faces; shadows would fall on the floor one moment, then creep toward the door the next. As soon as I stepped out in front of the audience into the center of the hall, my shadow darted toward the windowsill, tangling itself in the folds of the curtain. 
“The story must be born right here, before our very eyes,” said Vasya, holding out a box of matches. “Don’t stop talking until they’ve all burned out.”
A chill down my spine, a dry mouth—that’s how I feel when I step out under the spotlights. Usually, the play’s script serves as a highway from which there’s no turning off, but Vasya is asking me to create something new right here and now. 
The door opened, and a tall figure in a black coat appeared in the dim light of the hall. 
Sergei was late. He apologized profusely, greeted everyone noisily, and pulled funny faces. Turning to me, he beamed. 
“You came, too?!” he exclaimed joyfully. 
“Sergei, throw out a topic for a monologue,” Vasya asked him. 
Once, I stubbed out a cigarette on my shoulder, but I didn’t feel a thing. My skin was charred, and the hole was deep—as thick as a finger. The cigarette butt penetrated deeper and deeper into my body, and in the end, it was left sticking out of my shoulder like an ashtray. Lymph oozed from the wound, and I waited for it to finally start hurting. And all for the sake of performing as honestly as possible on stage. Sergei looked at me then with a mixture of astonishment, pity, and horror, and called me crazy.
 Now he looked at me differently, with extraordinary warmth. He was thinking seriously about the theme of the monologue, stroking his broad chest and scratching his unshaven chin.
“Tell me about your biggest disappointments,” he snapped his fingers. “What do you regret most in life?”
I shook the box.
“These matches won’t be enough,” I joked.
Memory is like a frayed roll of film. The years have jumbled the scraps and stuffed them into metal boxes. And it’s as if I’m sitting down at the editing table again…
“Are you taking the topic?” Vasya asked. “Does it resonate?”
I twirled a match in my hand but didn’t dare light it. I waited for the words to travel from my heart to my tongue and settle there obediently. 
“Want me to play along?” Sergei sat down at the piano and let his fingers fall onto the keys. “Go ahead, and I’ll pick up the rhythm and mood.” 
Definitely something new. Before, I was the one who used to play along with him, picking up the rhythm and matching his mood.
“Ooh! Is there going to be a soundtrack?” 
Where I’m from, there’s a strong belief: you mustn’t look into windows, or you’ll go blind. There’s a reason for that. For a Moldovan, the home is the center of the world. The devil himself built it first, but inside there was pitch-black darkness. A light-filled demiurge came to the rescue and cut windows into the walls, creating openings between the inner and outer worlds. Since then, the devil hasn’t been able to get inside the house. He freezes outside and glances enviously at the embroidered curtains.
	I stand next to the devil and watch the sky-blue house with its patterned window frames. There’s no place for me there anymore; it’s been taken by another Sasha, who looks exactly like me. In the house where I’m no longer welcome, the candles never go out and the hearth never grows cold. That other Sasha did everything right in life, and now a smile never leaves her eternally youthful face. But this house—it’s mine. Let me in!
Chirp…
authorBio: Alexa’s first novella was published in *Tolstoy* magazine, and her second made the long list for the *Lyceum* Award. Her writing explores the human soul: relationships between people, various forms of dependency, and the line between normality and pathology. Genre is secondary for Alexa—she writes in horror, science fiction, and fantasy, but she is particularly drawn to magical realism, gothic fiction, and family sagas.

title: The Order of (In)Justice
author: Nadya Hedwig
description:
Every employee of the nonprofit organization Wilde Jagd e.V. knows this: pity for the condemned is unacceptable, and doubt is forbidden. Executions take place strictly between 2:00 and 4:00 a.m.; Saturdays and Sundays are days off.

Martin Steinmeier, a young intern, is certain that if he doesn’t finally land a decent job, his chronic depression will drag him back down to rock bottom. Life will lose all meaning. 

Olga Orlova, the manager of Wilde Jagd, is convinced that as long as she works, her son—who has been seriously ill since birth—will remain healthy. That justifies everything. 

Ibrahim Zakaev, a senior employee at Wilde Jagd, is used to not asking unnecessary questions. When you’ve been on the run from your home country’s justice system for many years, any job will do. And those who’ve been sentenced deserve to die anyway.

They all believe they are serving the Great Justice. 
But does it even exist?..

story.quote: …what would your goodness be like if evil did not exist, and what would the earth look like if shadows disappeared from it?

excerpt:
This story began in a city that resembled a stone monster—indifferent and long dead, its guts splayed out along the river. The city is called Berlin, and living there—aside, of course, from the author, who conceived this whole story—is a certain Martin Steinmeier, a Russian-German originally from Kazakhstan. 
Martin was brought to Germany at the age of seven. Whenever he told anyone about it, he felt like a sack of potatoes that had been dragged across the border by a rope. He remembered little about the move: how his mom spent a long time trying to decide what to cram from their two-room apartment into a couple of small suitcases, how the border guard at the airport stamped his entry and gave him a reserved smile. How, two weeks later, his dad declared that Germany wasn’t for him and left. His mom, though, quickly found a replacement for him—she even said, “I found a replacement for your dad.” From her new husband, Martin inherited a rough Berlin accent and the resonant last name Steinmeier. 
In seventh grade, Martin fell into a depression, but then he seemed to snap out of it, and everyone decided it was just hormones. Whether it was hormones or not, from then on Martin was constantly afraid that his depression would return, that he would inevitably let someone down, and so he couldn’t finish a single thing he started. After high school, Martin enrolled at the Free University of Berlin, but dropped out after three semesters. He went on to train as a hairdresser, but six months before graduation, he decided that spending nine hours a day on his feet wasn’t for him. He decided to see the world and even set off on a round-the-world trip, but it didn’t last even a month: Martin contracted malaria and returned to Berlin. Back there, he was once again overcome by apathy, which God knows how it would have ended if not for the invigorating Berlin air and the pills prescribed strictly by a doctor. 
So at twenty-seven, Martin Steinmeier found himself an unlucky traveler, a man with little life experience, no notable achievements, and, as his mother put it, no decent profession. So it was no surprise that he was sent to the office of Frau Krause, an employee at the Berlin employment center. He had been there three times in the past year. The little room was small and white, with a single window overlooking a quiet courtyard and a cabinet where the files of her clients were kept.
This time, the room was the same, but instead of the slender Frau Krause, a lady so heavy that the chair beneath her seemed on the verge of breaking was sitting at the desk. 
The lady looked up from the monitor in front of her and gave Martin a cold stare. 
“Have a seat, Mr. Steinmeier.”
Just in case, Martin smiled at her. It didn’t work—the lady continued to play the role of the unapproachable Frau Helle from his least favorite fairy tale.
authorBio: Writer, philologist and literary scholar, literary consultant, and creative writing instructor.
— the "Great Maidens" trilogy (published by Chernym Belom),
— the novel *The Darkness Within You* (shortlisted for the 2025 Electronic Letter Award, to be published by Steklograf),
— Editor and curator of the short story collection *Trauma(s)*, based on the work produced in the author’s course “Accurate Depiction of Trauma in Literary Texts” (published by Steklograf)
In her work, she focuses on depicting psychological trauma and the experience of grief and loss, explores the nature of violence, and has been lecturing on these topics for more than three years.
"For herself," she reads psychological thrillers and social dramas. Her favorite contemporary author is Vera Bogdanova.
A source of inspiration for all time—M. S. Bulgakov’s *The Master and Margarita*, as well as the love story between Bulgakov and his third wife, Elena Sergeevna.

title: Everything That Remains
author: Sergey Kalinin
description:
Who it is for:

Readers who love deep psychological prose about broken lives, late chances, and people trying to find a way out of inner emptiness.

story.quote: ...how to answer that strange, unsettling question: what will remain after me?
about: Oleg has spent almost half his life in prison. Over the years he has lost everything: his family, his past, and himself. Once released, he wants to finish one last matter - a matter of honour. He will have to find the strength to repay debts to those who have long stopped waiting for him.

Dasha no longer believes her marriage can be saved. Routine, exhaustion, and a sense of inner emptiness have pushed joy out of her life. Beside her is a man who has long stopped striving for anything. And yet, somewhere deep inside, she still hopes that life can begin again.

Robert is used to keeping his life under control, but after an accident everything turns upside down. Now he has to return to the very beginning, and he has no right to weakness, because he is responsible not only for himself.

Three lives. Three people who have lost their footing.
What happens when their stories cross?
A novel about choice, inner strength, and the attempt to find oneself when everything seems lost.
excerpt: As usual, he stopped about twenty metres before the entrance. He looked around carefully and pretended to search for something in a large black bag. From here he could not be seen from the windows of the old five-storey building, yet he had a clear view of everything. Once he was sure there was no reason to worry, he quickly pulled on a jacket with a large, obscure Rem-zhilstroy inscription, which he had picked up at a construction site about a month earlier. He slung a bag over his shoulder, found there as well, one that looked very much like the kind carried by repairmen and utility workers. Now he could be an electrician, a plumber, or almost anyone else. Caution and attentiveness had long become the basic principles of his life. Especially now, when everything looked almost too good, he did not want to scare off luck with careless haste or confidence.
authorBio: Sergey Kalinin is a prose writer whose texts combine rare psychological precision with dense atmosphere. He writes about people at breaking points: when the familiar collapses and the new has not yet taken shape.

reviews.quote:
This book left not just warmth in my soul, but real inspiration. After books like this, you want to move mountains.

It has been a long time since a literary character inspired me so deeply.

The story is filled with light and faith in the better. After it, you are left with the feeling that even after the hardest trials, one can find the strength to keep going.
